title: Divide Intervals Into Minimum Number of Groups
statement:
Each `intervals[i] = [left_i, right_i]` is a closed range of integers, endpoints included. Split all the intervals into groups so that every interval belongs to exactly one group and no group holds two intervals that intersect. Return the smallest possible number of groups.

Two intervals intersect when some integer lies in both of them; touching at an endpoint counts, so `[1, 5]` and `[5, 8]` intersect.
notes:
## Intuition

If some integer lies inside k intervals, those k intervals all intersect each other, so they need k different groups. The surprising part is that this many groups is also enough: handle intervals by start and give each one any group whose last interval has already ended. So the answer is simply the largest number of intervals covering a single point. A brute force could try every grouping; a sweep over the number line finds the peak overlap directly.

## Approach

1. Turn each interval into two events: `+1` at `start` and `-1` at `end + 1`, the first point it no longer covers.
2. Sort events by `point`; on ties put `-1` first, so an interval ending just before a point is gone before another begins there.
3. Sweep the events, adding each `change` to `active`, the number of intervals covering the current point.
4. The largest `active` seen, `best`, is the answer.

## Example 1, step by step

Intervals `[5,10], [6,8], [1,5], [2,3], [1,10]` give sorted events `(1,+1) (1,+1) (2,+1) (4,-1) (5,+1) (6,-1) (6,+1) (9,-1) (11,-1) (11,-1)`.

`active` goes `1, 2, 3, 2, 3, 2, 3, 2, 1, 0`, so `best = 3`: at point 2, for instance, `[1,5]`, `[2,3]` and `[1,10]` all overlap.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n log n) to sort the 2n events; the sweep is linear.
- Space: O(n) for the events.

## Pitfalls

- Endpoints are inclusive: `[1,5]` and `[5,8]` share 5, so the end event goes at `end + 1`, not `end`.
- With the end at `end + 1`, process `-1` before `+1` at the same point; otherwise `[1,4]` and `[5,8]` would look like they overlap.
- Do not merge intervals or count disjoint chains; only the peak overlap matters.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `events` | `[point, change]` pairs: `+1` where an interval starts, `-1` just after it ends |
| `point`, `change` | the current event's position and effect |
| `active` | intervals covering the current point |
| `best` | the highest overlap seen, which is the minimum number of groups |

narration.3: Look at each interval's two ends.
narration.4: The interval starts covering points at start.
narration.5: It stops covering points at end + 1, because end itself is included.
narration.7: Sort by position, and at the same position let endings come before starts.
narration.11: Sweep the number line from left to right, one event at a time.
narration.12: Update how many intervals cover the current point.
narration.13: Keep the largest overlap seen so far.
narration.15: The peak overlap is exactly the number of groups needed.
